lines: A smokehouse tells you fast who understands patience.
Empty hooks before supper can <shake>frighten</shake> a village more than thunder.
Salt is patient. That's why it keeps food better than most people keep promises.
Empty hooks tell a village to start worrying before anyone says it aloud.
People think about courage until supper is late. Then they think about supper.
A village with good stores can make careful choices instead of desperate ones.
Most days, I am at the smoker, trying to keep clean cuts from becoming everyone else's problem.
People think meat is simple until something goes wrong and suddenly it is very important.
I trust a good cleaver more than a loud promise. The cleaver has less to prove.
Fresh work starts before anyone smells the smoke.
A clean table matters more than a loud promise around here.
You learn respect for food when waste has a face and a cost.
Good stores keep a village calm through bad weather.
People notice the butcher only when the shelves are empty or the smoke is wrong.
There is care in this work, even if outsiders only see the knife.
Salt, smoke, timing, and steady hands. That is the honest shape of the day.
A village with full stores argues less about tomorrow.
I do not rush sharp work. Rushed sharp work remembers you.
The best cuts are planned before the blade moves.
Meat spoils faster than gossip, but both need watching.
I keep count because hunger never accepts vague answers.
Good curing is patience with a practical smell.
The smokehouse teaches you to notice small changes quickly.
A careful butcher feeds more people than a proud one.
When you had me follow you, I kept thinking the whole walk needed a sharper plan.
I remember that road by the meals we missed along it.
The village smoke vanished behind us sooner than I expected.
I should have asked where we were going before I packed for half the distance.
You kept a hard pace. At least you also kept looking back for me.
I spent the first night wondering whether the smokehouse door was still latched.
Next time I am bringing more dried food and fewer hopeful guesses.
Every empty stretch of road made the next roof look inviting.
I learned which of your warnings mean hurry and which mean drop everything.
The food bag felt lighter long before my feet did.
I slept with my cleaver close and still woke at every sound.
You knew where to find water when my own plan had run dry.
I kept thinking about the stores I had left behind.
The smell of woodsmoke on the way home nearly stopped me in my tracks.
My legs recovered quickly. My appetite took no time at all.
I would follow you again, but I would ask about the route over supper first.
That journey taught me what a locked smokehouse door is worth.
I remember sharing the last good ration beside the road.
We came home with ourselves and our supplies. That is enough for me.
The first meal back tasted better because nobody had to eat it while walking.
A boat ride beats being dragged over rough ground. I still prefer cutting across town, not <aqua><wavy>water</wavy></aqua>.
That crossing taught me to pack food that will not roll under a bench.
I watched the shore disappear and wondered who was minding the smoker.
You made rowing look calm while I counted every leak twice.
Salt spray got into the food bag, my sleeves, and somehow my boots.
The water was quiet enough to hear my stomach complain.
I kept one hand on the supplies whenever the boat tipped.
Land looked better after that trip than any feast table ever has.
Next time the jerky goes in a sealed sack.
I learned not to stand just because something moved beyond the oar.
The waves slapped the hull all night and spoiled every chance of sleep.
You trusted that little boat more than I trust a borrowed cleaver.
I could not see what moved below us, and I liked it that way.
We rationed the food before we knew how far the current had carried us.
The first tree on shore looked sturdy enough to hug.
I was soaked through, but the provisions stayed mostly dry.
Even after landing, the chopping block seemed to sway under my hands.
I would cross again with a clearer sky and twice the rope.
The boat brought us home. I stopped insulting it after that.
A hot meal on solid ground settled me better than any reassurance.
Sharp knives are not angry knives. That is the first lesson.
A village eats better when nobody mistakes haste for skill.
I know every sound a clean cut should make. I also know when the street sounds wrong.
Most days begin with washing the block and checking yesterday's stores.
Fresh meat gives you a short time to make good decisions.
I trust a balanced cleaver because it never asks me to admire it.
An empty hook tells me more than a crowded market does.
The smoker has a loose rattle on windy mornings. I know when it changes.
One dirty knife can waste more food than an empty pantry.
I sharpen before the edge is dull enough to argue.
The animals stay calmer when the work yard stays quiet.
Salt is cheap compared with losing a whole cut.
I keep the clean cloths where wandering hands cannot find them.
A butcher who cannot count should stay away from the winter stores.
Smoke needs watching even when it looks settled.
I would rather trim carefully than explain waste to a hungry family.
Every hook gets cleaned before anything new goes on it.
Good work leaves the table ready for tomorrow.
The last task is always checking the latch.
I know the day went well when supper arrives without anyone asking how.
